claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr contains matrix and incipient precipitate or interfacial phases with different thermal expansion coefficients.
Differential thermal expansion between these phases generates interfacial residual stresses.
The mismatch-generated residual stresses alter local dislocation mobility.
The mismatch-generated residual stresses alter phase stability or interfacial microstructure.
Residual stresses from thermal expansion mismatch govern the stress–strain response of HfNbTaTiZr.
Residual stresses from thermal expansion mismatch govern the thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr.
Residual stresses from thermal expansion mismatch govern high-temperature creep in HfNbTaTiZr.
Residual stresses from thermal expansion mismatch govern post-aging hardening in HfNbTaTiZr.
Conventionally processed HfNbTaTiZr naturally contains incipient or nanometric precipitates embedded in a high-entropy matrix.
Thermal cycling or high-temperature loading causes the matrix and precipitates to expand at different rates.
The resulting local residual stresses accelerate creep at the highest tested temperatures.
The resulting local residual stresses reinforce strain hardening during aging.
The resulting local residual stresses alter the temperature dependence of the elastic modulus.
Increasing thermal expansion mismatch will increase the creep rate at 1250 °C relative to unmodified HfNbTaTiZr.
Increasing thermal expansion mismatch will produce anomalous or nonlinear elastic-modulus behavior between 293 K and 1100 K.
Increasing thermal expansion mismatch will increase hardening after aging at 600–800 °C.
Reducing thermal expansion mismatch will moderate the proposed creep, modulus, and age-hardening effects.
Thermal-mismatch effects are minimal below 600 °C.
Thermal-mismatch effects are significant from approximately 600 °C to 1250 °C.
Above 1250 °C, diffusion or phase-instability mechanisms may dominate over thermal-mismatch residual stresses.
